capitulo.titulo: 2.1 (II) · Growth, carrying capacity and human impact

visual.texto: Carrying capacity is the average size of a population determined by competition for limited resources.

turnos.t: Second half: how a population grows.
Think of an island with deer.
The island can only support, say, about a hundred and sixty of them.
That limit is the carrying capacity, shown with the letter K.
Your teacher's definition: carrying capacity is the average size of a population determined by competition for limited resources.
Or: the maximum population size sustainably supported by an environment.
It isn't fixed.
It changes if resources, conditions or interactions change.
And why do individuals compete?
Because of limiting factors: the resources in the environment, such as water, nutrients and sunlight, that are needed for survival.

visual.veredicto: Only density-dependent factors regulate a population around K

turnos.t: Limiting factors come in two types.
Density-dependent limiting factors tend to regulate the population size around the carrying capacity.
They get stronger as density rises: more individuals means more competition, more spread of disease and more predation.
Density-independent limiting factors affect every population regardless of its size or abundance: storms, hard frosts, droughts or fires.
An exam example: a flood kills forty percent of a population of voles, whether there are a hundred or ten thousand.
Because the effect doesn't depend on how many there are, it's density-independent.
Ask yourself: does it get worse when there are more individuals?
If the answer is yes, it's density-dependent.
First model: the J-curve.
If there are no limiting factors, the population grows exponentially.
That's exponential growth.
Each step adds more individuals than the one before, and the graph shoots up in the shape of a J.
The example from class is yeast.
It has very simple needs, and if you give it all the food, water, oxygen, space and warmth it needs, it grows exponentially.
Your teacher links this to r-strategists.
But it can't last: resources run out and the population collapses.
That's the crash.
Second model: the S-curve, or logistic growth.
Here limiting factors do act, and there are four phases.
Lag: few individuals, slow growth.
Exponential phase: there are plenty of resources and the population shoots up.
Transitional phase: close to the carrying capacity, competition increases and growth slows down.
And plateau: the population levels off at the carrying capacity, with births roughly equal to deaths, in a steady-state equilibrium.
Example: most large mammals.

If you're asked to distinguish them, for two marks: J-shaped is exponential growth when no limiting factors act, ending in a crash, whereas S-shaped is logistic growth that slows as density-dependent factors increase and levels off at carrying capacity.

pasos: Death rate up, birth rate down
visual.nota: Below K the reverse happens: steady state around K

turnos.t: Many real populations combine both curves.
They grow exponentially, go past the carrying capacity, which is the overshoot, and then oscillate around it until they settle.
The overshoot happens because of time lags: the effect takes a while to show.
What brings them back is a negative feedback loop.
Above the carrying capacity there's more competition, so the death rate goes up and the birth rate goes down.
Below it, the opposite happens.
A real case, Activity 8: the snowshoe hare and the Canada lynx.
This is predation, and each one limits the other: more hares, more lynx; more lynx, fewer hares; and with fewer hares, fewer lynx.
If the lynx went extinct, the hares would be regulated by food, competition and disease instead.
There are two reproductive strategies.
r-strategists have lots of small offspring, reproduce early, live short lives and give little parental care.
Their numbers rise fast and fluctuate.
They do well when disturbance is frequent: dandelions, mosquitoes, annual plants.
K-strategists have few, larger offspring, reproduce later, live longer and care for their young a lot.
They stay close to the carrying capacity.
They do well in stable conditions with strong competition: elephants and albatrosses.
It's a continuum, not rigid boxes.
And watch out for a trap: don't write that a J-curve equals an r-strategist.
The shape of the curve depends on whether limiting factors act.
A dandelion in a stable garden can follow an S-curve.

escenas.titulo: The human population and its K

turnos.t: The human population went from about one billion in 1800 to seven point eight billion in 2020, and reached eight billion in 2022.
We've removed many limiting factors: agriculture, sanitation, medicine and technology have increased survival and resources.
But the human carrying capacity is very hard to calculate, for four reasons.
Technology in farming, fossil fuels and groundwater has expanded it artificially.
Global trade moves food, energy and materials around, so local capacity doesn't depend on local resources.
Consumption varies enormously from person to person.
And non-biodegradable waste degrades ecosystems.
Our niche keeps changing all the time.

visual.titulo: An ecosystem as an open system
visual.nota: Resilience rises with biodiversity, redundancy and storages

turnos.t: Ecosystems are systems, just like we saw in Topic 1.
They're open systems: sunlight, water and nutrients come in, and heat and matter go out.
Their parts are interdependent: if one changes, the others change too.
They have storages, like biomass, soil and leaf litter.
And they have emergent properties, like natural goods and ecosystem services.
What increases their resilience?
High biodiversity and functional redundancy, large and varied storages, and feedback that helps them recover.
But a severe or long-lasting disturbance, natural or human, can push an ecosystem past a tipping point.
One example is deforestation in the Amazon, which reduces moisture recycling.

visual.pie: Sea otter eating a sea urchin: it protects North Pacific kelp forests
visual.credito: matt knoth · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

turnos.t: Some species matter far more than their numbers suggest.
Keystone species are species that regulate how an ecosystem works to an extent that a large effect on its stability is noticed when their population decreases.
If they disappear, they set off a trophic cascade.
The star example: the sea otter of the North Pacific eats sea urchins.
Without otters, urchin numbers rise, they wipe out the kelp, and the kelp forest collapses, leaving many species without a habitat.
Two more, from Activity 11.
The purple sea star eats mussels: remove it, and the mussels take over the whole rock and diversity falls.
And the African elephant keeps the savanna open, disperses seeds and digs water holes that other animals use.
Last block: human impact.
Biosphere integrity is a planetary boundary with two dimensions.
Genetic diversity: the safe limit is fewer than ten extinctions per million species per year.
Today it's a hundred or more, with about a million species threatened.
Functional integrity: the safe limit is for us to take ten percent of the energy plants produce, and we take thirty percent.
The threats are direct, like overexploitation or poaching, or indirect, like habitat loss, climate change, pollution and invasive species.
The responses: conservation, which prevents degradation and protects species in situ or ex situ, and regeneration, which actively restores ecosystems, for example through rewilding.

filas: No limits + crash vs levels off at K
Above K, below K, negative feedback

turnos.t: For the exam, here are the typical questions.
The define questions: species, population, community, niche, carrying capacity, keystone species.
Word for word.
Density-dependent regulation, four marks: name the factors, say what happens above the carrying capacity, what happens below it, and mention negative feedback.
The sea otter, three marks: it eats urchins; without otters the urchins wipe out the kelp; that's a trophic cascade.
And the six-mark question: discuss whether the human population levelling off around 2100 means we're approaching carrying capacity.

Six ideas: the projection is due to lower fertility and an ageing population; it's a demographic trend, not an ecological limit; technology changes the limiting factors; consumption per person matters; use an indicator, like the ecological footprint; and finish with a balanced conclusion.
